content.problem: A sensor model says that a future reading has mean \(2\) and standard deviation \(3\). What should a finite collection of simulated readings look like, and how can we check our simulator? We will compare independent formulas with JAX samples, then deliberately underflow a likelihood calculation. This is the numerical foundation for the Bayesian model in the next lesson.
content.idea: A distribution describes variability in outcomes. Averaging independent observations can reduce uncertainty in their mean without removing the spread of individual outcomes. Keep these two uncertainties on separate labels and scales.
objectives: Distinguish samples, density, variance and standard error
Check normal moments against independent analytic expectations
Use log-space arithmetic for an extreme mixture likelihood
Demonstrate both key replay and independent split-key draws

sections.title: A precise mean does not make individual outcomes predictable
sections.body:
For independent readings with standard deviation \(3\), the sample mean of \(100\) readings has standard deviation \(3/\sqrt{100}=0.3\), while a new reading still has standard deviation \(3\). The first quantity describes variation in an average across repeated samples; the second describes the data-generating spread of individual values.

The displayed standard-error curve is calculated from the independence assumption, not estimated from repeated experimental batches. Positive correlation would make \(2/\sqrt{N}\) too optimistic because the effective amount of independent information is smaller. Before using a narrow band, identify whether its random quantity is a mean, parameter or future observation.

check.prompt: Does a tenfold smaller standard error mean future individual observations are ten times less variable?
check.answer: No. Standard error concerns the estimator of the mean. The observation distribution can retain the same variability.

sections.title: Start with units, not an API
sections.body: A standard deviation has the same units as a sensor reading. Variance has squared units. To change a standard-normal draw \(z\) into a reading, multiply by the standard deviation and add the mean: \(x=2+3z\). The expected variance is \(9\), not \(3\). This is why the scale parameter in our log-density divides the residual before squaring. We assume a strictly positive finite scale; validation belongs at a public input boundary.

sections.title: One draw and a sample average answer different questions
sections.body: A single future reading has standard deviation \(3\). An average of \(N\) independent readings has standard error \(3/\sqrt{N}\). More simulation improves an estimate of the model mean; it does not make the next sensor reading less noisy. At \(N=20000\), the mean standard error is about \(0.0212\). Our deterministic seeded test uses a generous five-standard-error bound and a separate variance check. A statistical tolerance can fail by chance for other seeds, so keep the seed, sample size and actual discrepancy.

sections.title: Logarithms preserve ratios that densities lose
sections.body:
A probability density is not the probability of observing one exact real-valued reading. Density has inverse-reading units, and probability comes from integrating it over an interval or region. For example, the normal density at its peak can exceed one for a sufficiently small standard deviation without violating probability rules.

A normal log-density is a negative quadratic plus normalization terms. Summing log-densities for independent observations avoids multiplying many small values. A mixture instead adds weighted densities, so use log-sum-exp: for component log-densities \(-1000\) and \(-1001\), subtracting the maximum before exponentiation preserves their relative contribution. The executed stable mixture log density is about \(-1000.380\); direct exponentiation underflows at this scale even though the log result remains finite.

sections.title: A random key is part of the experiment
sections.body: Calling a random function twice with the same key and shape replays the same values in this tested environment. It does not create two independent samples. Split the key before assigning it to separate draws. NumPy and JAX need not return matching random arrays for the same integer seed: compare distributional properties, not bit patterns across libraries. Our sample checks establish a small numerical example, not a universal test of a random-number generator.

content.output: The sample mean is close to \(2\), the variance is close to \(9\), and the stable mixture log-density is approximately \(-1000.38\).
content.exercise: Change the sensor to mean \(-1\), standard deviation \(0.5\), and draw \(30000\) readings from a new key. Predict the variance and the standard error of the sample mean, then verify both moments.
content.solution:
# Exercise solution
# Create or split explicit PRNG key(s) (`changed`) for reproducible randomness.
changed = -1.+.5*jax.random.normal(jax.random.key(51),(30000,))
assert abs(float(changed.mean())+1.) < 5*.5/math.sqrt(30000)
assert abs(float(changed.var())-.25) < .015
content.question: Which statement explains why a large Monte Carlo sample can have a precise mean while individual readings remain variable?
options: Every sample becomes equal to the mean as sample size increases
The variance of each reading is divided by the sample size
The standard error of the average decreases, while the distribution of an individual reading stays the same
content.explanation: For independent draws the average has variance \(\sigma^2/N\); a new reading still has variance \(\sigma^2\). These are different random variables.
content.diagnosis: If the simulated variance is near three instead of nine, inspect whether you multiplied by sqrt\(3\) when the stated scale was three. If two supposedly independent arrays match exactly, inspect key reuse before changing the distribution. If a mixture likelihood becomes negative infinity, compare the log-sum-exp result before widening dtype.

experiments.title: Density can exceed one
experiments.prediction: For a normal with standard deviation \(0.1\), can its density at its mean exceed \(1\)?
experiments.code:
# Experiment — Density can exceed one
peak = jnp.exp(normal_logpdf(0.,0.,.1))
assert peak > 1
print("peak density:",float(peak))
experiments.explanation: A narrow continuous density can exceed one; its area, not its height at a point, sums to one.

experiments.title: Separate sum and mixture
experiments.prediction: Do two independent observations with log densities \(-2,-3\) have the same log likelihood as one equal mixture of those components?
experiments.code:
# Experiment — Separate sum and mixture
values = jnp.array([-2.,-3.])
independent_log = values.sum()
mixture_log = logsumexp(values)-jnp.log(2.)
assert jnp.allclose(independent_log,-5.)
assert mixture_log > -3.
print(float(independent_log),float(mixture_log))
experiments.output: The independent joint log likelihood is \(-5\); the mixture log density is approximately \(-2.38\).
experiments.explanation: Independence multiplies probabilities, while alternative mixture components add weighted probabilities.

practice.title: Detect a missing normalization
practice.prompt: Compare scales \(1\) and \(2\) at their common mean. Show why a residual-only objective incorrectly ties them.
practice.hint: The residual is zero for both; retain \(-\log\sigma\).
practice.solution:
# Detect a missing normalization (Transfer / diagnosis): Scale changes density even with identical zero residuals.
scores = normal_logpdf(0.,0.,jnp.array([1.,2.]))
assert jnp.allclose(scores[0]-scores[1],jnp.log(2.))
practice.explanation: Scale changes density even with identical zero residuals.

practice.title: Demonstrate key ownership
practice.prompt: Produce two separately owned standard-normal draws and show replay of the first. Explain why replay alone does not test independence.
practice.hint: Split before use; compare arrays with the same shape.
practice.solution:
# Demonstrate key ownership (Transfer / diagnosis)
# Create or split explicit PRNG key(s) (`(left, right)`) for reproducible randomness.
left,right = jax.random.split(jax.random.key(17))
# Sample deterministic random values into `first` using an explicit PRNG key.
first = jax.random.normal(left,(32,))
# Sample deterministic random values into `second` using an explicit PRNG key.
second = jax.random.normal(right,(32,))
assert jnp.array_equal(first,jax.random.normal(left,(32,)))
assert not jnp.array_equal(first,second)
practice.explanation: Different split keys avoid accidental replay; one differing pair does not prove every statistical property of a generator.

takeaways: A density is not a point probability.
Moment checks need sample size, units and a justified tolerance.
Log-space arithmetic and explicit keys make likelihood experiments inspectable.

visual.title: A precise mean does not remove observation noise
visual.prediction: Which band shrinks when we increase the number of independent observations?
visual.reading: The horizontal axis is independent sample count \(N\) on a logarithmic scale, so equal horizontal steps multiply sample size by the same ratio. The vertical axis is standard deviation in sensor-reading units. The individual-reading curve stays at 3; the sample-mean curve is \(3/\sqrt{N}\), reaching 0.3 at \(N=100\). These are analytic standard deviations under independence, not observed confidence-interval coverage.
visual.connection: At \(N=100\), averaging reduces uncertainty about the mean by a factor of ten but does not shrink the spread of the next reading. The seeded sample check reports mean 2.0067 and variance 9.0353, close to the model values 2 and 9 for this finite draw. Correlated draws would not follow the same standard-error curve without accounting for dependence.
visual.alt: A precise mean does not remove observation noise. The horizontal axis is the number of independent observations on a logarithmic scale: equal spacing represents equal ratios of sample sizes. The vertical axis is the standard deviation in sensor-reading units. The flat curve stays at \(3\): it describes one reading. The decreasing curve is \(3/\sqrt{N}\): it describes the average of \(N\) readings. At \(N=100\), the average has standard deviation \(0.3\), ten times smaller than an individual reading. These curves are analytic quantities evaluated by the executed example, not measured coverage intervals.

content.code:
# Step 1 — 1. Define a density and its contract
import math
import numpy as np
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
from jax.scipy.special import logsumexp

def normal_logpdf(value, loc, scale):
    return -0.5*((value-loc)/scale)**2 - jnp.log(scale) - 0.5*jnp.log(2*jnp.pi)

# Step 2 — 2. Sample with explicit ownership
# Create or split explicit PRNG key(s) (`(key_a, key_b)`) for reproducible randomness.
key_a, key_b = jax.random.split(jax.random.key(23))
# Sample deterministic random values into `a` using an explicit PRNG key.
a = 2. + 3.*jax.random.normal(key_a, (20000,))
# Sample deterministic random values into `b` using an explicit PRNG key.
b = 2. + 3.*jax.random.normal(key_b, (20000,))
expected_mean, expected_variance = 2., 9.
assert abs(float(a.mean())-expected_mean) < 5*3/math.sqrt(a.size)
assert abs(float(a.var())-expected_variance) < .4
assert not jnp.array_equal(a,b)
assert jnp.array_equal(a, 2.+3.*jax.random.normal(key_a,(20000,)))

# Step 3 — 3. Compare an independent calculation
actual = normal_logpdf(jnp.array([2.,5.]),2.,3.)
reference = [-math.log(3*math.sqrt(2*math.pi)), -.5-math.log(3*math.sqrt(2*math.pi))]
np.testing.assert_allclose(actual,reference,rtol=1e-6)
components = jnp.array([-1000.,-1001.])
stable = logsumexp(components)-jnp.log(2.)
assert jnp.isfinite(stable)
assert jnp.isneginf(jnp.log(jnp.exp(components).mean()))
print('sample mean, variance:',float(a.mean()),float(a.var()))
print('stable equal-mixture log density:',float(stable))

buildSteps.explanation: The normalization term matters when comparing different scales; the squared residual alone is not a density.

buildSteps.title: 2. Sample with explicit ownership
buildSteps.instruction: Append the sampler. Split one parent key before drawing two samples; retain each array so replay and variation can be checked.

optionFeedback: The mean becomes more precisely estimated while individual draws remain variable. Compare the sampling distribution with the distribution of sample means.
Dividing variance by sample count describes uncertainty in the mean estimator, not the variability of one future reading.
For independent draws the average has variance \(\sigma^2/N\); a new reading still has variance \(\sigma^2\). These are different random variables.
